that too would be an iniquity for the judges,
for I would have denied God above.

“If I have been glad at the downfall of him who hated me,
or lifted myself up because evil had found him—

but I have not let my palate sin
by asking for his life with a curse—

if the people of my household have never said,
‘Is there anyone who did not get his fill of Job’s meat?’

the sojourner has not lodged in the street;
my doors I have opened to the traveler{f}—

if I have covered my transgressions like Adam,{g}
by hiding my iniquity in my bosom,

because I feared the crowd,
or the scorn of clans frightened me,
and so I kept quiet and stayed inside—

O that I had one to hear me!
Here is my mark;{h} let Shaddai answer me!
And the scroll that my adversary has written—

surely on my shoulder I would bear it;
I would bind it on myself as crowns.

The number of my steps I would declare to him;
like a prince I would draw near to him.

“If my land cries out against me,
and its furrows weep together,

if I have eaten its yield without payment,
or caused the soul of its owners to breathe out,

notes.text: Or “my crops.”
That is, the widow. The Hebrew of this verse is uncertain.
Hebrew qanah, “reed,” here the upper arm bone.
That is, the sun.
An ancient gesture of worship toward the sun or moon.
So the ancient versions; the Hebrew reads “to the road.”
Or “as men do”; Hebrew ʾadam.
Hebrew taw, the last letter of the Hebrew alphabet, written as a cross-shaped mark; here, Job’s signature on his sworn statement.
Hebrew boʾshah, found only here; some noxious weed, perhaps cockle. The identification is uncertain.

verses.text: So these three men ceased to answer Job, because he was righteous in his own eyes.
Then the anger of Elihu{a} the son of Barachel{b} the Buzite,{c} of the family of Ram, was kindled. Against Job his anger was kindled, because he declared himself righteous rather than God.
And against his three friends his anger was kindled, because they had found no answer, and yet had condemned Job.{d}
Now Elihu had waited to speak to Job, because they were older in days than he.
And when Elihu saw that there was no answer in the mouth of the three men, his anger was kindled.

And Elihu the son of Barachel the Buzite answered and said:
“Young am I in days,
and you are very old;
therefore I held back and was afraid
to declare my knowledge to you.

I said, ‘Let days speak,
and let the multitude of years make wisdom known.’

But truly it is a spirit in man,
and the breath of Shaddai, that makes them understand.

It is not the many in years{e} who are wise,
nor the aged who understand what is right.

Therefore I say, ‘Listen to me;
let me declare my knowledge, I also.’

Yes, I gave you my close attention,
and see, there was none who refuted Job,
none among you who answered his words.

Beware lest you say, ‘We have found wisdom;
God may vanquish him, not man.’

He has not directed his words against me,
and with your speeches I will not answer him.

“They are dismayed; they answer no more;
words have departed from them.

And must I tarry, since silent they are,
since idle they stand, replying no further?

I too will answer my share;
I too will declare my knowledge.

For I am full of words;
the spirit within my belly constrains me.

Inside, I am like wine with no outlet,
like new wineskins about to burst.

Let me speak, that I may find relief;
let me open my lips and answer.

Let me not, I pray, show partiality to any man,
nor use flattering titles toward any man.

For I do not know how to give flattering titles;
else my Maker would soon take me away.

notes.text: Elihu means “He is my God.” He is the only speaker in the book whose name is a clearly Israelite one.
Barachel means “God blesses.”
Buz was a son of Nahor, Abraham’s brother (Genesis 22:21); compare Jeremiah 25:23. The Septuagint adds “of the country of Ausis” (Uz) (Brenton).

So the standard Hebrew text. According to an ancient Jewish tradition this is one of the “corrections of the scribes,” and the original read “and so had condemned God,” that is, by failing to answer they had in effect put God in the wrong.
So the Septuagint, Syriac, and Vulgate; the Hebrew reads “the great.”

verses.text:
“But now hear, O Job, my speech,
and to all my words give ear.

See now, I have opened my mouth;
my tongue in my palate speaks.

Upright of heart are the sayings I utter;
plain knowledge my lips shall pour forth.

The Spirit of God has made me,
and the breath of Shaddai gives me life.

If you are able, answer me;
set your words in order before me; take your stand.

See, I am toward God as you are;
from clay I too was nipped off.{a}

See, dread of me need not terrify you,
nor my pressure{b} be heavy upon you.

“Surely you have spoken in my ears,
and the sound of your words I heard:

‘Clean am I, without transgression;
pure{c} am I, and there is no iniquity in me.

See, he finds occasions{d} against me;
he counts me as his enemy.

In the stocks he sets fast my feet;
over every path of mine he keeps watch.’

Lo, herein you are not just—so I reply—
for mightier than mortal is God.

Why do you contend against him,
saying that he answers none of man’s{e} words?

Once God utters it, yes, twice,
yet it is unheeded by man:

then he uncovers the ears of men
and seals their instruction,{f}

to turn man aside from his deed
and to conceal pride from a man;

he keeps back his soul from the pit,
and his life from passing over by the javelin.{g}

“He is also chastened with pain upon his bed,
and with continual strife in his bones,

till his very life abhors food,
and his appetite the choicest dish.

His flesh is consumed away from sight,
and his bones, once unseen, are laid bare.

And his soul draws near to the pit,
and his life to those who bring death.{h}

Should there stand by him a messenger,
an interpreter,{i} one out of a thousand,
to make plain to a man his uprightness,

let his flesh become fresher{j} than a child’s;
let him return to the days of his youthful vigor.

He has ransomed my soul from going down to the pit,
and my life will see the light.’

“See, all these things God works,
twice, three times, with a man,

to bring his soul back from the pit,
so that the light of life may shine on him.

Attend, O Job; hearken to me;
hold your peace while I talk.

If you have words, answer me;
speak, for I desire to justify you.

If not, then hearken to me;
keep still, and wisdom I shall impart.”

notes.text: That is, pinched off, as a potter takes a piece of clay.
Hebrew ʾekef, found only here; perhaps “pressure” or “burden.”
Hebrew ḥaf, found only here; “clean” or “innocent.”
Or “pretexts”; Hebrew tenuʾot, a rare word.
Hebrew “his”; perhaps “answers for none of his own deeds.”
Or “frightens them with warnings”; the Septuagint reads “he scares them with such fearful visions” (Brenton); the Hebrew is uncertain.
Or “crossing the river (of death)”; Hebrew shelaḥ can mean a weapon or a channel.
Or “to the angels of death,” or “to the place of the dead.”
Hebrew melits, an interpreter or spokesman; compare 16:20. The Septuagint reads “Though there should be a thousand messengers of death, not one of them shall wound him” (Brenton).
Hebrew rutafash, found only here; the meaning “grow fresh” is a guess from context.
Or “it was not worth it for me.”

verses.text: Then Elihu answered and said:

“Hear my words, you wise men,
and you who know, give ear to me;

for the ear tests words
as the palate tastes food.

Let us choose for ourselves what is right;
let us know among ourselves what is good.

For Job has said, ‘I am righteous,
and God has taken away my right;

though in the right, I am reckoned false;
past healing is my wound,{a} though there is no offense in me.’

What man is like Job,
who drinks up scoffing like water,

and goes in company with the workers of iniquity
and walks with men of wickedness?

For he has said, ‘A person gains nothing
by delighting in God.’

“Therefore, you men of heart,{b} hear me:
far be it from God that he should do wickedness,
and from Shaddai that he should do wrong.

For he repays people for what they do
and brings upon each the results of his own conduct.

Surely, of a truth, God will not do wickedly,
and Shaddai will not pervert justice.

Who entrusted the earth into his keeping?
Who set in place{c} the entire world?

If he should set his heart upon himself,{d}
and gather to himself his spirit and his breath,

all living creatures would die together,
and humanity would go back to dust.

“If you have understanding, hear this;
listen to the sound of my words.

Shall even one who hates justice govern?
And will you condemn the Righteous Mighty One,

who says to a king, ‘Worthless one!’
to nobles, ‘Wicked man!’

who lifts not the face of rulers,
nor sets the wealthy ahead of the lowly,
since every one is wrought by his hands?

For his eyes are upon the ways of a man,
and he sees all his steps.

There is no darkness nor deep shadow
where the workers of iniquity may hide themselves.

God does not need to examine anyone further
before bringing him to judgment.

He shatters the mighty without inquiry
and sets others in their place.

Because he knows what they do,
he overthrows them in the night, and they are crushed.

As wicked men he strikes them
in the place where all can see,{e}

because they turned aside from following him
and did not consider any of his ways,

so that they caused the cry of the poor to come to him,
and the cry of the afflicted he heard.

If he stays silent, who can condemn him?
If he hides his face, who can see him,
whether nation or individual alike?

that a godless man should not reign,
that there be no snares for the people.{f}

“For has a man ever said unto God,
‘I bore my correction; no more will I transgress;

what I do not see, teach me;
if I have done iniquity, I will do it no more’?

Men of understanding will tell me so,
and every sage who gives me a hearing:

‘Job speaks without knowledge,
and his words are without insight.’

Would that Job were tried to the end,
because of his answers like men of iniquity!

notes.text: Hebrew “my arrow,” that is, the wound made by God’s arrow (compare 6:4).
That is, men of understanding; so also 34:34.
Hebrew lacks “on him.”
Or “If he should set his mind on it”; the Hebrew is uncertain.
Hebrew “in the place of the onlookers.”
The Hebrew of verses 29–33 is very obscure.
A gesture of scorn.

verses.text: Then Elihu answered and said:

“Do you count this to be just?
You say, ‘My righteousness is more than God’s,’

that you ask, ‘What advantage is it to you?{a}
What profit is mine more than if I had sinned?’

I will answer you with words,
and your friends with you.

Look to the heavens, and see;
and behold the clouds, which are higher than you.

Should you sin, how do you strike at him?
Be your rebellions many, what harm is that to him?

Be you just, what gift is that to him?
What does he take out of your hand?

To a man like you your wrongdoing reaches,
to a mortal your uprightness.

“Because of the multitude of oppressions they cry out;
they call for help because of the arm of the mighty.

Yet none asks, ‘Where is God who fashioned me,
who grants songs in the night season,

who teaches us more than the beasts of the earth,
and makes us wiser than the birds of the heavens?’

So they cry aloud, and he gives no reply,
by reason of the haughtiness of the evil.

Surely God does not hear an empty cry,
nor does Shaddai regard it.

How much the less when you claim you behold him not,
that your plea lies before him, and you wait upon him!

And now, since his wrath has not visited,
and he takes little note of folly,{b}

Job opens his mouth in vain;
he multiplies words without knowledge.”

notes.text: That is, to Job himself, “you” referring to himself in quoting his complaint; or, “to me.”
Hebrew pash, found only here; the meaning is uncertain, perhaps “folly” or “transgression.”

verses.text: And Elihu continued and said:

“Bear with me a little, and I will show you,
for there are yet words to say on God’s behalf.

I will bring my knowledge from far away
and credit my Maker with justice.

For truly my words are not false;
one perfect in knowledge is with you.

“See, God is mighty, and does not despise any;
mighty in strength of heart.

The ungodly he lets not live,
but to the lowly he grants justice.

He does not withdraw his eyes from the righteous,
but with kings upon the throne
he seats them forever, and they are exalted.

Should they lie bound in chains,
held fast by the ropes of misery,

then he declares to them their work
and their transgressions, that they have behaved proudly.

He opens their ear to discipline
and commands that they return from iniquity.

If they obey and serve him,
they will finish their days in prosperity
and their years in pleasure.

But if they do not listen, they pass over by the javelin{a}
and breathe their last without knowledge.

“The godless in heart store up anger;
even when he binds them, they do not call for help.

Their soul dies in youth,
and their life among the cult prostitutes.{b}

He delivers the afflicted by his affliction
and opens their ear by oppression.

But you are full of the judgment of the wicked;
judgment and justice take hold of you.

Take care lest fury lure you to mockery,
and let not a great bribe lead you astray.

Can your outcry set you beyond trouble,
or every effort of your might?

Do not long for the night,
when peoples are cut off in their place.

Watch yourself; turn not toward evil,
since that you prefer above affliction.

“See, God is exalted in his power;
who is a teacher like him?

Who has appointed him his way?
Or who can say, ‘You have done wrong’?

Remember to magnify his work,
of which men have sung.

All mankind has looked upon it;
man beholds it from afar.

See, God is great, and we know him not;
the number of his years is past searching out.

For he draws up the drops of water;
they distill rain from his mist,

which the clouds pour down
and shower upon mankind abundantly.

Can anyone understand the spreading of the clouds,
the crashings of his pavilion?

See, he spreads his light about him
and covers the roots{d} of the sea.

For thereby he rules the nations;
plentiful food he bestows.

He covers his hands with the lightning
and commands it to strike the mark.

Its crashing declares concerning him;
the cattle also, concerning what rises.{e}

notes.text: Or “cross the river (of death)”; see the note at 33:18.
Hebrew qedeshim, men who served as prostitutes at pagan shrines; the sense here is that their lives end in shame.
The Hebrew of verses 16–20 is very obscure.
Or “the depths.”
The Hebrew of this verse is very obscure. The Septuagint reads “The Lord will declare concerning this to his friend: but there is a portion also for unrighteousness” (Brenton).

verses.text:
“Yes, at this my heart quakes
and springs up from its seat.

Hear, O hear the rumbling of his voice,
and the murmur that goes out from his mouth.

He sends it out under the whole sky,
and his lightning to the ends of the earth.

God thunders wondrously with his voice;
he does great things, and we cannot know them.

For he bids the snow, ‘Come down upon the earth,’
likewise the shower of rain, his torrents of strong rain.

He seals up the hand of every man,
that all men whom he made may know it.{b}

Then the beast goes into its lair
and remains in its dens.

Out of its chamber comes the storm,
and cold from the scattering winds.{c}

By the breath of God ice is given,
and the breadth of the waters is frozen fast.

He loads the thick cloud with moisture;
the cloud scatters his lightning.

They turn round and round by his guidance,
to do whatever he commands them
upon the face of the habitable world.

Whether for correction, or for his land,
or for steadfast love, he causes it to come.

“Give ear to this, O Job;
stand still and consider the wonders of God.

Know you how God charges them,
and makes the lightning of his cloud blaze out?

Do you know the balancings{d} of the clouds,
the wonders of him who is perfect in knowledge,

you whose clothes grow warm
when the land lies hushed beneath the south wind?

Can you join him in spreading out the sky,
hard as a mirror of cast metal?

Teach us what we shall say to him;
we cannot set our case in order because of darkness.

Should he be told I want to speak?
Would anyone ask to be swallowed up?

Now no one can look at the sun,
brilliant as it is in the sky,
once the wind has passed and swept the clouds away.

Out of the north comes golden splendor;{e}
about God is awesome majesty.

Hence mortals hold him in awe;
none of the wise in heart does he regard.”{f}

notes.text: Hebrew “them.”
Or “that all men may know his work”; the Hebrew is uncertain.
Hebrew mezarim, “scatterers,” perhaps the north winds; uncertain.
Hebrew miflese, found only here; perhaps “spreadings” or “balancings.”
Or “golden light.” The Septuagint reads “From the north come the clouds shining like gold” (Brenton).
Or “all the wise of heart cannot see him.”

verses.text: Then Yahweh answered Job out of the whirlwind{a} and said:

“Who is this that darkens counsel
by words without knowledge?

Gird up now your loins like a man;{b}
I will question you, and you shall make it known to me.

“Where were you when I founded the earth?
Declare it, if you have understanding.

Who fixed its measurements—surely you know!
Or who stretched the line upon it?

Upon what were its footings settled,
or who set down its cornerstone,

when the morning stars sang together
and all the sons of God{c} shouted for joy?

“Or who shut in the sea with doors,
when it burst forth from the womb and went out,

when I made the cloud its garment
and thick darkness its swaddling band,

and broke for it my boundary
and set bars and doors,

and decreed, ‘To here you may come, but not beyond;
here your swelling waves must halt’?

“Have you, in your days, commanded the morning,
or caused the dawn to know its place,

so that it grasps the edges of the earth
and shakes the wicked out of it?

It is changed like clay under the seal,
and things stand out like a garment.{d}

And from the wicked their light is withheld,
and the uplifted arm is broken.

“Have you entered into the springs of the sea,
or walked in the recesses of the deep?

Have the gates of death been revealed to you,
or have you seen the gates of deep darkness?

Have you comprehended the breadth of the earth?
Declare, if you know it all.

“Where is the way to where light dwells,
and darkness, where is its place,

that you might lead it to its border
and know the roads to its dwelling?

You know, for you were born then,
and the number of your days is great!{e}

“Have you entered the storehouses of the snow,
or have you seen the storehouses of the hail,

which I have reserved for the time of distress,
for the day of battle and war?

By what way is the light{f} parted,
or the east wind scattered upon the earth?

“Who carved a course for the flooding rain,
a road for the thunder’s bolt,

to bring rain on a land where no man is,
on the wilderness in which there is no human being,

to satisfy the waste and desolate ground,
and to make the tender grass spring forth?

Is there a father for the rain?
Who sired the dewdrops?

From whose womb came the ice?
And the hoarfrost of heaven, who has given it birth?

The waters hide themselves as if turned to stone,
and the face of the deep is locked fast.

“Can you bind the bonds of the Pleiades,{g}
or loosen the cords of Orion?{h}

Can you lead forth the Mazzaroth{i} in its season,
or guide the Bear{j} with its children?

Do you know the statutes of the heavens?
Can you establish their rule upon the earth?

“Can you raise your voice to the clouds
so that a deluge of water covers you?

Can you send forth lightnings, that they may go
and say to you, ‘Here we are’?

Who has put wisdom in the ibis,{k}
or given understanding to the rooster?

Who by wisdom counts the clouds?
Who tips over the jars of heaven,

when the dust runs into a mass
and the clods cleave fast together?

“Can you hunt the prey for the lion,
or satisfy the appetite of the young lions,

as they couch within their lairs,
or lurk in ambush in the thicket?

Who readies for the raven its prey,
when to God its nestlings call
and stray about without food?

notes.text: Or “storm.”
Or “like a warrior”; Hebrew gever.
The Septuagint reads “all my angels praised me with a loud voice” (Brenton). See the note at 1:6.

The image is of the dawn bringing the shapes of the earth into relief, as a seal impresses clay. The Septuagint reads very differently: “Or did you take clay of the ground, and form a living creature…?” (Brenton, modernized).
Irony: Yahweh grants Job, in jest, the age of creation itself.
Or “lightning.”
Hebrew kimah, a cluster of stars, generally identified as the Pleiades; Brenton’s Septuagint has “Pleias.” Compare 9:9.
Hebrew kesil, “fool,” generally identified as Orion, pictured as a giant bound in the sky. The identifications of these constellations are traditional, not certain.

Hebrew mazzarot, found only here; perhaps the constellations of the zodiac, or a particular star or constellation (compare mazzalot, 2 Kings 23:5). The Septuagint keeps “Mazuroth” and adds “the evening star with his rays” (Brenton).
Hebrew ʿayish, perhaps the Great Bear (Ursa Major) with its “children,” the stars of its tail; others suggest Aldebaran or the Hyades. Compare 9:9.

Hebrew tuḥot and sekhvi (“rooster”) are both rare and uncertain; others render “in the inward parts… to the mind.” The ibis (sacred to the Egyptian god of wisdom) and the rooster (heralding the dawn) were both regarded as weather-wise birds. The Septuagint reads “who has given to women skill in weaving, or knowledge of embroidery?” (Brenton).

verses.text:
“Do you know the time when the mountain goats{a} give birth?
Do you watch over the calving of the does?{b}

Can you reckon the months they complete,
or know the season of their bearing,

when they crouch, bring forth their young,
and cast out their labor pains?

Their young ones grow strong; they grow up in the open field;
they go forth and do not return to them.

“Who sent out the wild donkey{c} free?
Who has loosed the bonds of the swift donkey,

to whom I gave the steppe as dwelling,
and the salt waste as his abode?

It scorns the noise of the town
and does not hear a driver’s shouts.

He ranges the mountains as his pasture
and searches after every green thing.

“Will the wild ox{d} consent to be your servant?
Will he lodge beside your feeding trough?

Can you bind the wild ox in the furrow with his rope?
Or will he harrow the valleys after you?

Will you trust him because his strength is great,
and leave to him your labor?

Will you trust him to haul in your seed
and heap it upon your threshing floor?

“The ostrich{e} flaps its wings with joy,
but are its feathers and plumage like the stork’s?{f}

For she abandons her eggs upon the ground
and leaves them to warm in the dust,

forgetting that a foot may crush them,
and the wild beast trample them.

She deals harshly with her young, as if they were not hers;
though her labor be in vain, she has no fear,

since God has deprived her of wisdom
and allotted her no discernment.

When she rouses herself to flee aloft,{g}
she laughs at the horse and his rider.

“Is it you who grant the horse his strength?
Is it you who robe his neck with a mane?{h}

Do you make him leap like the locust?
The splendor of his snorting is terror.

It paws{i} the ground in the valley and rejoices in its power;
it charges out to face the weapons.

At fear he scoffs, undaunted;
from the sword he turns not away.

Upon him rattles the quiver,
the flashing spear and the javelin.

Quivering and raging he devours the distance;
when the horn blows he will not hold still.

At each blast of the horn he cries, ‘Hurrah!’
From far off he scents the fight,
the captains’ thunder and the battle cry.

“Does the hawk{j} take flight by your wisdom
and stretch his wings toward the southland?

Is it at your command that the eagle{k} mounts up
and makes his nest on high?

On the cliff he dwells and lodges,
on the tooth of the crag and the stronghold.

From there he spies out the prey;
his eyes behold it afar off.

His young ones also suck up blood,
and where the slain are, there is he.”

notes.text: Hebrew yaʿale salaʿ, “climbers of the rock,” probably the Nubian ibex. Brenton’s Septuagint has “wild goats of the rock.”
Hebrew ʾayyalot, female deer; Brenton has “hinds.”
Hebrew pereʾ, and in the next line ʿarod (found only here in the Hebrew Bible), both names for the wild ass or onager, a swift, untamable desert animal.
Hebrew reʾem, the aurochs or wild ox (now extinct), a powerful horned animal; the Septuagint has monokerōs, rendered “unicorn” by Brenton and other older English versions.

Hebrew renanim, found only here, “cries” or “shrieking ones,” generally taken as the ostrich, which fits the description that follows. The Septuagint reads “The peacock has a beautiful wing: if the stork and the ostrich conceive…” (Brenton). The identification is probable but not certain.
Or “are they the pinions of the kindly one?” Hebrew ḥasidah (stork) sounds like ḥesed, “steadfast love.” The Hebrew of this line is uncertain.
The meaning of the Hebrew verb is uncertain.
Hebrew raʿmah, found only here; perhaps “thunder,” “quivering,” or “a mane.” Brenton’s Septuagint has “terror.”
Hebrew “They paw.”
Hebrew nets, a falcon or hawk; the hawk’s southward migration may be in view.
Hebrew nesher, which can refer to the eagle or the griffon vulture; verse 30 suits the vulture.

verses.text: And Yahweh answered Job and said:

“Shall a faultfinder contend with Shaddai?
He who argues with God, let him answer it.”
Then Job answered Yahweh and said:

“See, I am of small account; what shall I answer you?
My hand I lay upon my mouth.

Once I have spoken, and I will not answer;
twice, and I will proceed no further.”
Then Yahweh answered Job out of the whirlwind and said:

“Gird up now your loins like a man;
I will question you, and you shall make it known to me.

Will you even annul my justice?
Will you condemn me, that you may be righteous?

Do you have an arm like God’s,
or a voice that thunders like his?

“Deck yourself now with majesty and dignity;
clothe yourself with splendor and honor.

Let loose the floods of your wrath;
behold each proud one, and bring him down.

Look on everyone who is proud, and bring him low,
and tread down the wicked where they stand.

Hide them in the dust together;
bind their faces in the hidden place.

Then I also will acknowledge to you
that your own right hand can save you.

“Behold now Behemoth,{a} whom I made along with you;
like cattle he feeds on grass.

See now, his strength is in his loins,
and his power in the muscles of his belly.

He stiffens his tail like a cedar;
the sinews of his thighs{b} are knit together.

His bones are tubes of bronze,
his limbs like bars of iron.

“It ranks first among God’s works;{c}
only its Maker can approach it with his sword.

For the mountains bring forth produce for him,
where all the beasts of the field play.

Under the lotus trees{d} he lies,
in the covert of the reed and the marsh.

The lotus trees cover him with their shade;
the willows of the brook surround him.

If the river surges, it is not alarmed;
it stays calm even if the Jordan{e} rushes up to its mouth.

Can he be seized while he watches,
or his snout be pierced with a trap?

notes.text: Hebrew behemot, the plural of behemah, “beast,” used here as an intensive: “the Beast” par excellence. The description best suits the hippopotamus, though some see the elephant or a mythical creature. The Septuagint reads “But now look at the wild beasts with you” (Brenton, modernized). The identification is uncertain.
Hebrew paḥad, here probably “thighs” (an Aramaic sense); found in this sense only here. Some take it as “testicles.”
Or “the chief of God’s works.” The Septuagint reads “This is the chief of the creation of the Lord; made to be played with by his angels” (Brenton).
Hebrew tseʾelim, found only here and in verse 22; probably the thorny lotus (Ziziphus lotus). Brenton’s Septuagint has “trees of every kind, by the papyrus, and reed, and bulrush.”
That is, any great river in flood.

verses.text:
“Can you draw out Leviathan{a} with a fishhook,{b}
or press down his tongue with a cord?

Can you put a rush rope in his nose,
or pierce his jaw with a hook?

Will he plead with you at length?
Will he address you gently?

Will he make a covenant with you,
that you take him for a servant forever?

Will you play with it as with a bird
or keep it on a leash for your girls?

Will partners haggle over him?
Will they parcel him out among the traders?

Can you stuff his hide with barbs,
or his skull with fish-spears?

Set your hand on him once;
think of the fight—you will do it no more!

“See, the hope of a man is disappointed;{c}
is he not laid low even at the sight of him?

No one is fierce enough to stir it up.
Who, then, can stand against me?

Who has given me something first, so that I must repay?{d}
Everything under all the heavens belongs to me.

“I will not stay silent about its limbs,
its great strength, or its graceful build.

Who can strip off his outer garment?
Who can come within his double coat of mail?{e}

Who can open the doors of his face?
Round about his teeth is terror.

His back is ranks of shields,{f}
sealed up tight together.

One is so near to another
that no air can come between them.

Each to its fellow is joined;
they grip one another and will not be parted.

His sneezings flash forth light,
and his eyes are like the eyelids of the dawn.{g}

From his mouth burning torches stream;
fiery sparks spring out.

From his nostrils smoke pours,
as from a seething pot over kindled reeds.

Its breath sets coals ablaze,
and flames shoot from its mouth.

In his neck abides strength,
and before him dances dismay.

The folds of its flesh are tightly joined,
firm on it and immovable.

His heart is firm as a stone,
firm as the nether millstone.

At his rising the mighty{h} take fright;
at the crashing they lose themselves.

The sword that strikes it is useless,
as are the spear, the dart, and the javelin.{i}

He counts iron as straw,
and bronze as rotten wood.

No arrow drives him off;
sling stones become chaff to him.

Clubs are counted as stubble;
he laughs at the rattle of the javelin.

Beneath him are jagged shards;
like a threshing sledge he sprawls in the mud.

He makes the deep boil like a pot;
he makes the sea like a pot of ointment.

It leaves a gleaming trail behind it;
you would think the deep had turned white-haired.

Upon earth there is not his like,
a creature made without fear.

He beholds everything that is high;
he is king over all the sons of pride.”{j}

notes.text: Hebrew livyatan; see the note at 3:8. Here the description is often thought to draw on the crocodile, but it is enlarged with features of the mythic sea dragon (fire-breathing, verses 18–21), and the identification remains uncertain. The Hebrew and the Septuagint (Brenton) number 41:1–8 as 40:25–32, and 41:9–34 as 41:1–26. Brenton’s Septuagint begins with the question whether one can catch the serpent with a hook (Brenton, modernized).
Or “a hook.”
Hebrew “his hope is false,” that is, the hope of anyone who would attack him.

The Hebrew of verses 10–11 is difficult; some manuscripts and the Septuagint have a third-person sense, “who can stand before him… who has confronted him and come away safe?” (reported). Compare Romans 11:35.
So the Septuagint, “who can enter within the fold of his breast-plate?” (Brenton); the Hebrew reads “his double bridle,” perhaps referring to the jaws.
Or “His pride is his rows of shields.” The Hebrew gaʾavah, “pride,” and gav, “back,” differ by vowels only.
The Septuagint reads “At his sneezing a light shines, and his eyes are as the appearance of the morning star” (Brenton).
Or “the gods.”
Hebrew shiryah, found only here; perhaps “javelin” or “coat of mail.”
Hebrew bene-shaḥats, also at 28:8; probably the proud beasts of prey. The Septuagint reads “and he is king of all that are in the waters” (Brenton).

verses.text: Then Job answered Yahweh and said:

“I know that you can do all things,
and that no purpose of yours can be thwarted.

‘Who is this that hides counsel without knowledge?’
Therefore I declared what I did not understand,
things too wonderful for me, which I did not know.

‘Listen, and I will speak;
I will question you, and you will inform me.’

By the hearing of the ear I had heard of you,
but now my eye sees you;

therefore I despise myself,{a}
and I repent{b} upon dust and ashes.”
After Yahweh had said these things to Job, Yahweh said to Eliphaz the Temanite, “I am angry with you and your two friends, because you have not spoken what is right about me, as my servant Job has.

So now take seven bulls and seven rams for yourselves, and go to Job my servant, and offer up for yourselves a burnt offering. And Job my servant will intercede for you, for his prayer I will accept, so as not to treat you as your folly deserves; because you have not spoken rightly concerning me, as has Job my servant.”
So Eliphaz the Temanite and Bildad the Shuhite and Zophar the Naamathite went and did as Yahweh had told them, and Yahweh accepted Job.
And Yahweh turned the captivity{c} of Job when he prayed for his friends. And Yahweh gave to Job twice as much as all that he had before.

Then all his brothers and sisters and all his former acquaintances came to see him, and they shared a meal with him in his house. They felt sorry for him and consoled him over all the calamity that Yahweh had brought on him. Each one gave him a piece of money{d} and a gold ring.{e}
And Yahweh blessed the latter end of Job more than his beginning. And he had fourteen thousand sheep, and six thousand camels, and a thousand yoke of oxen, and a thousand female donkeys.
He had also seven sons{f} and three daughters.
And he called the name of the first Jemimah,{g} and the name of the second Keziah,{h} and the name of the third Keren-happuch.{i}
And in all the land no women were found so fair as the daughters of Job. And their father gave them an inheritance among their brothers.
And after this Job lived a hundred and forty years,{j} and saw his sons, and his sons’ sons, four generations.
And Job died, old and full of days.{k}

notes.text: Or “I reject (my words),” or “I melt away”; the Hebrew verb has no stated object. The Septuagint reads “Wherefore I have counted myself vile, and have fainted” (Brenton). This verse is a well-known crux.
Or “I am comforted,” or “I relent concerning dust and ashes,” that is, concerning my mortal condition or my mourning. The Hebrew niḥamti can bear several senses.
Or “restored the fortunes.”

Hebrew qesitah, a unit of money or weight of unknown value, found elsewhere only in Genesis 33:19 and Joshua 24:32; the Septuagint has “a lamb” (Brenton), and some ancient versions also take it as a lamb. The Qumran Aramaic Targum of Job (11QtgJob) is reported to end in this verse.
Or “a nose ring” or “earring.” The Septuagint reads “four drachms’ weight of gold, even of unstamped gold” (Brenton).
The Hebrew form shivʿanah is unusual; some Jewish interpreters took it to mean “twice seven,” that is, fourteen sons.
Jemimah probably means “dove”; the Septuagint has “Day” (Brenton).
Keziah means “cassia,” a fragrant spice; the Septuagint has “Casia” (Brenton).
Keren-happuch means “horn of eye-paint,” a container for the cosmetic used to darken the eyelids; the Septuagint has “Amalthæa’s horn” (Brenton), the horn of plenty.
The Septuagint reads “And Job lived after his affliction a hundred and seventy years: and all the years he lived were two hundred and forty” (Brenton).

The Septuagint adds a long postscript (Brenton, modernized): “And it is written that he will rise again with those whom the Lord raises up. This man is described in the Syriac book as living in the land of Ausis, on the borders of Idumea and Arabia, and his name before was Jobab. And having taken an Arabian wife, he fathered a son whose name was Ennon. And he himself was the son of his father Zare, one of the sons of Esau, and of his mother Bosorrha, so that he was the fifth from Abraham. And these were the kings who reigned in Edom, which country he also ruled over: first, Balac the son of Beor, and the name of his city was Dennaba; and after Balac, Jobab, who is called Job; and after him Asom, who was governor out of the country of Thaeman; and after him Adad the son of Barad, who destroyed Madiam in the plain of Moab, and the name of his city was Gethaim. And his friends who came to him were Eliphaz, of the children of Esau, king of the Thaemanites; Baldad, sovereign of the Sauchaeans; Sophar, king of the Minaeans.” This addition identifies Job with Jobab of Genesis 36:33 and is not part of the Hebrew text.
